newsitem.title: INDIA: Cotton-India futures trade seen poised for takeoff.
newsitem.headline: Cotton-India futures trade seen poised for takeoff.

text.p: The formation of a new government in India and the expected passage of the federal budget for 1997/98 (April/March) is expected to clear the way for launching futures trading in cotton soon, traders said on Thursday.
Inder Kumar Gujral, the new prime minister of the United Front (UF) coalition government, won a parliamentary vote of confidence last week after the defeat of the alliance's previous regime.
The cabinet of the new government had adopted the much-acclaimed budget of the UF's previous government, unveiled on February 28.
The budget proposes to reintroduce futures trading in cotton after a gap of nearly 30 years.
Futures trading in key commodities, including cotton, was banned in the early 1960s in a bid to curb speculation and stabilise prices.
"The smooth passage of the budget will ensure the launch of futures trading in cotton within a couple of months," said a trader. "What remains is only a formality."
A debate on the budget, which began on Wednesday, is expected to last until May 16.

Cotton trading in April, as in the case of most commodities, had been dull following the political crisis, triggered by the withdrawal of crucial support by the Congress Party to the minority UF government on March 30.
"Demand for cotton from yarn mills had also been very limited because of poor yarn prices abroad," the trader said. Indian cotton yarn mills export large quantities of yarn.
Traders said they would expect cotton prices to remain steady, moving in a narrow range, in the current week on limited demand and supply.
"While demand for cotton from yarn mills is poor, supply of quality cotton is equally tight," said one trader.
Traders said the bulk of the 1996/97 (October/September) crop, estimated at 16 million bales (one bale is 170 kg) had already arrived in the market.
"Whatever is left with the farmers, government agencies and traders will come in small lots as and when prices firm up further," the trader said.

In the week to Wednesday prices of most cotton varieties remained more or less steady. Bengaldeshi was quoted at 860/920 rupees per maund (32.37 kgs). Punjab saw-ginned was offered at 1,560/1,590 rupees per maund.
Gujarat Kalyan was quoted at 13,200 rupees per candy (355.56 kg). Gujarat Wagad was steady at 12,600 rupees per candy.
